text: — Well, wait now, let me tell you how we went with Bay Ganyo to the exhibition in Prague — said Tsvyatko with a smile.
— Bravo, Tsvyatko! — we all shouted. — We’ve been waiting for this for so long!
Tsvyatko began:

— If you remember, we set off from Sofia with a whole train of our own carriages and our own locomotive. Carriages of only 1st and 2nd class, brand-new, just arrived from Europe, impeccably clean and comfortable. In the same carriage, there were compartments of both 1st and 2nd class. A multitude of people—were we 160 souls, I don’t remember. Old, young, women, men, children, and even infants. (Oh, those infants!...)

Who is like us! What pride it was that we were setting off for the exhibition with our own train. Let the Europeans see, we told ourselves, that Bulgaria is not asleep. But most of all, we puffed ourselves up with the novelty, the modern construction, and the cleanliness of the carriages. But for how long, do you think, did we enjoy the patriotic charm of the superiority of our carriages and the thought that we would stun Europe with our progress? As long as they were seeing us off at the station, as long as we were passing the Slivnitsa and Dragoman positions—the fields of our glorious victories—our enthusiasm grew proportionally with the emptying of the bottles and the baskets of provisions with which the practical tourists had abundantly supplied themselves. “Of course, we’ll take snacks; why should we give our money to the Serbs?” shouted Bay Ganyo, inspired by patriotism and Pleven wine. But as we approached Tsaribrod and it began to get dark, as they tried to light the carriages and it turned out they had forgotten to prepare the lamps, as it grew completely dark, as the children began to get scared and wail—oh, then little by little, as if with the slipping away of Bulgarian territory, our patriotic enthusiasm was slipping away too. Some smiled sadly, others smiled with hidden sarcasm (we weren't only Bulgarians), others were indignant; even Bay Ganyo whispered in my ear: “Does a pig understand spring water!” Some, meanwhile, let out unambiguous curses directed at a foreigner serving in the management of our railways. Supported by the latter, Bay Ganyo cried out: “Don’t I know that we aren't to blame, it’s those foreigners again, devil take them! They did it on purpose to disgrace us! And do you realize, it’s all out of envy! They’re all like that!”

With these words, he gave one of the foreigners such a look that it made him cough and move to the next compartment. When we stopped at the station in Tsaribrod, it was pitch black in the carriages; we couldn't even see one another. We got agitated, we got angry, and then we turned it into a joke. A host of jokes and barbs were directed at our railway officials. Shouts were heard: "Give us some candles, people, the children are terrified!", "Hey, old man, go buy us a pound of candles, we'll give you a tip!", "Come on, at least give us a single tallow candle!" Only Bay Ganyo refused to entertain the possibility that Bulgarians could be responsible for such mismanagement.

— That one over there, do you see him — he was saying, after they had brought a few simple candles, pointing at one of our own "foreigners," — you should drench him in tar and set him ablaze. Is this to be endured! Never mind the darkness, who cares about that—but we’ve become a disgrace before the Serbs. There he is, look at him, a Serbian official—the man is laughing. He’s laughing, and no wonder! But his aroused patriotism would not allow Bai Ganyo to endure a Serb smirking at him, so he scowled back at him:
— And why are you laughing there, hey! And he wanted to jump out of the carriage and go have it out with the Serb. Heroic blood!
— Shh... Behave yourself, Bay Ganyo — the passengers urged him — don't make a scene. Bear in mind that you are entering Serbia...
— Well, so what if I'm entering Serbia! Are they going to scare me? What about Slivnitsa? What about "backwards, brothers" — and a curse flew out of Bay Ganyo's mouth like a bomb.
— How is the Serb to blame that our carriages are dark! — the others were calming him down.
— Who? Him? I know their kind! — answers Bay Ganyo, shaking his head.

They handed out one candle per compartment. Some lamps, I think, they managed to adjust and light. The train set off. The passengers dripped hot tallow on the windows and fixed the candles. This was the first   B u l g a r i a n i z a t i o n   of the new carriages. The second Bulgarianization took place during the very first night: all the toilets (pardon me, gentlemen) were turned into cesspools.

Anyway, we made it through Serbia. But don't you think for a moment that we passed through it just like that—quietly and modestly. Oho! The Bulgarian is no fool! Wherever there was an opportunity, Bay Ganyo didn't miss a chance to needle the Serbs, to remind them of Slivnitsa. In Niš and Belgrade, he even asked all the officials and porters: "Aren't you Bulgarian? Tell the truth! You're all Bulgarians, you're just acting like Serbs."

We set off across Hungary!... And here, the wheels of one carriage caught fire! To hell with your "experts"! We were stopped for a long time. They doused it, extinguished it, it flared up, it smoldered... finally, we got moving. And the Magyars—how they laughed! They knew!—Bulgarian tourists!... And at one more spot, that carriage caught fire again—finally, they left the damn thing for repairs.

Bay Ganyo, an experienced man who had traveled before, was telling his simpler companions:
— Now we’re heading for Pest. Once we pass Pest—Vienna; Prague is beyond Vienna. I’ve scoured all those places—I know them like the back of my hand.

We did not stop at the small stations. At the large ones, we stopped only long enough for the line to be cleared. Wealthy Moravia caught everyone’s attention. The beautifully cultivated valleys, the magnificent gardens, the countless factories and plants made even Bay Ganyo concede Moravia’s superiority over our homeland: “We work too, but these fellows aren’t lagging behind either; no, they aren’t lagging behind, they know their stuff, these fellows.” But realizing he had been carried away by his praise, he added: “But it’s all for nothing. They do the work, and the German eats it.”

Along the way, things didn't pass without some comedy. We — I, Vancho, Filyo, and Ivanitso's son (I don't believe you know him) — occupied a first-class compartment; in the neighboring second-class section, Bay Ganyo settled in with several companions, richly supplied with provisions. Bay Ganyo, out of haste, it seems, had forgotten to put any snacks in his saddlebags. "Well, after all, we are Bulgarians, we'll look out for one another. A piece of bread from this one, a bit of cheese from that one — a man will get by. Why not!" And indeed, he got by quite well. His companions treated him to food and drink — he treated them to the most fervent patriotism, mixed with appetite and thirst. But everything has an end. Finally, our neighbors' provisions ran out, and the demijohns were emptied. (To avoid a gross error, I must correct myself: the demijohns were emptied while we were still flying past Slivnitsa and Dragoman with "Long live Bulgaria, hurrah! Let me wet my whistle, man, hurrah!")

Bay Ganyo began to insinuate himself into our compartment. At first, he sought various pretexts: now he would ask for matches, then for a glass of cognac—claiming his stomach was bothering him—and then, little by little, he made himself at home, grew accustomed to us, and, one might say, hardly ever left our little room. He forgot his companions, and why should he care for them anyway? "They have nothing—everything eaten, everything drunk," while with us, thank God, there was always a little something to be found—we would buy things at the stations. Bay Ganyo, out of curiosity, never missed a chance to sample the foreign products:
— What's this, is it grapes? Bravo! Look! Give me a little bunch. Mmm! Good! Bravo! Curiosity drove him to acquaint himself in this manner with our snacks, our cognac, and our cigarette cases.
— "Is that cigarette case made of Caucasian silver?" Bay Ganyo inquired curiously, seeing one of us preparing to light up.
— It isn't, it's of Viennese make! — the owner replies.

— Is that so? Let me see it. Tsk, tsk, tsk! Look at that! And there’s tobacco, too—Bulgarian, isn’t it? Bravo! Wait, let me roll a cigarette. I have cigarette papers; if you ever need any, I’m right here!

That he was here, we felt it quite strongly: by the smell of his boots, by the specific aroma of his sweaty body, and by his aggressive movement toward occupying the entire sofa. At first, he sat on the very edge of the sofa; then he began to seat himself more comfortably; later, three of us had to squeeze onto one sofa, and Ivanitsov’s son had to huddle on the edge of the other, so that Bai Ganyo could stretch out horizontally. And he never missed an opportunity. We agreed to test just how far Bai Ganyo’s need for comfort could go, and he began, in all sincerity, to feed our curiosity:

— Move over a bit towards the edge so I can put my other leg up too. That’s it! Bravo! Ahhh! Damn it all! Pure bliss! Just listen to what the engine is doing: chug-chug, chug-chug! It’s flying!... I love stretching out like this. It’s cramped over there. And the companions—simple folk, what is there to talk about with them?... What are you eating there, a pear? Bravo! Let’s see if I can eat a pear while lying down like this. Thank you! Where do you get these things from?
— We’ll buy them — one of us answers, barely containing himself.
— Is that so? Bravo! — he approves with his mouth full of juicy pear. — I love pears.

Bay Ganyo, lulled by the monotonous rhythm of the locomotive, began to doze. I was thinking what, what trick we could play on him. Finally, a brilliant thought struck me. I signaled to my companions beforehand and said:
— Let’s make some coffee, gentlemen. Hand over the spirit and the stove.
— Coffee? — cried Bay Ganyo and jumped from the sofa as if stung. — You don't say!
— How are we to make coffee? There is no water — Ivanitso's son spoke up with theatrical affectation.
— "Water?" Bay Ganyo shouted in the same voice. "Just ask me for water. Right away!" — And he flew out of the compartment.

We were dying of laughter. Ivanitso’s son stretched out and took up the whole sofa. Bai Ganyo returned, huffing and puffing more than was necessary. He had to show us what toil and trouble he had endured for our sake. In his hand was a small pitcher.

— There, I found it, did you see? I scoured all the carriages! Finally, I see a pitcher, I grabbed it in a flash, and a woman shouted at me: “Hey, give the water here, it’s for my child.” What lie to tell, what lie to tell, then it hit me: “Excuse me, madam, someone over there has fainted.” “Is that so,” she says. “It is.” “Well, then take him the water quickly and bring the little pitcher back.” Simpleton of a woman!... Phew! I broke a sweat. Now, how about a little coffee!
— Aren't you ashamed, sir! — said one of the companions reproachfully, who could no longer contain his indignation.

Bay Ganyo looked at him with a strained face, trying to portray his sincere astonishment as vividly as possible; after that, quite unexpectedly, he said:
— It did cross my mind that the whole thing was a setup, but "oh well," I said. Well then, give me at least a cigarette and a little cognac.

We gave him a cigarette and a cognac, and he went back to his compartment, to the simple folk. "These scholars are terrible fools," Bay Ganyo’s voice was heard a moment later in the next compartment; "I don’t know how they tolerate such people in the civil service. But just you wait, your Bay Ganyo will return to Bulgaria, and then we shall see who’s who."

We were approaching the Czech border. Traveling with us were the commissioners sent by the government to learn how an exhibition is organized, so that they could organize the one in Plovdiv as well. One of them pinned small Bulgarian tricolors to the chests of all the passengers. Along the way, a rumor spread that we would be greeted ceremoniously both at the border and in Prague; consequently, we were prepared for the encounter—but what we saw in reality surpassed all our expectations.

Here is the border station; the locomotive is already whistling. We see, to the left and right of the railway, crowds of people streaming toward the station. It was drizzling, and the running men, women, and children carried open umbrellas. We came to a halt. The platform was jammed with people. Immediately, a band struck up "Shumi Maritsa." A choir then sang "Kde domov muj" to the infinite pleasure of us all, and especially of Bay Ganyo, who praised the Czech people among us for having learned the tune of the Bulgarian folk song "Where is my kin" quite well, except that they pronounced the words a bit unclearly, so they weren't very easy to understand.

Blood rushes to my head with shame when I recall the way we behaved during that first encounter. Imagine, gentlemen: the whole city had gathered, people had come from the villages to welcome their Bulgarian brothers; they brought a band, a choir had come, a multitude of girls had lined up with bouquets in hand, waiting for the "brothers" to step off the train so they could welcome them, greet them with words, with songs, with music, with flowers; but the "brothers" just stuck their heads out of the windows and stared! Believe me, believe me, gentlemen! The carriage windows, you must know, are narrow; one had poked his head out, another was huddling over his shoulder, a third was peeking from below, showing only half a distorted face with a single eye—and they just stared! — It was enough to make you die of embarrassment! Oh, if only there had been a snapshot camera! — The welcoming party was bewildered. They didn't know what to do—where to put the bouquets! The music stopped, the choir stopped, and a silence fell as everyone just stared at each other.

At one point, Bay Ganyo got off the carriage. All the Czechs fixed their eyes on him and made way for him to pass, and he passed... Good God! How pompously Bay Ganyo walked amidst hundreds of eyes and hands reaching out to him with bouquets. He set off, twirling his left mustache with his whole palm, thrust out his elbows, coughed deeply, and glanced with one eye at the young lady who had held her bouquet almost under his nose; he looked at her and wiggled the fingers of his left hand, turned upwards, as if to say: "Are you welcoming me, girl, are you? You're doing well, keep welcoming, I like it" — and went on his way without deigning to honor her by accepting her bouquet. The girl sheepishly pulled back her hand. After a while, Bay Ganyo reappeared, ungracefully buttoning a part of his attire. Again they made way for him, again he twirled his left mustache, again he coughed, blew his nose with his fingers, and climbed into the carriage. The locomotive whistled and we set off.

Lest any of you think that I am exaggerating, that I am intentionally embellishing my narrative to caricature Bay Ganyo, I will tell you that, on the contrary, I am omitting certain things, because even now my heart sinks when I recall them. For instance, I kept silent at the very beginning about the sight our train presented as early as the second day of our journey. I believe I mentioned that our tourists had dragged their infants along with them; leaving aside the crying and the screaming, I will tell you that the lavatories had been turned into laundries where they washed the children's soiled little shirts and drawers, and the corridors of the carriages were turned into drying rooms for this laundry: they strung up ropes and hung out the none-too-cleanly washed drawers: these replaced the flags with which we were supposed to decorate our train; instead of the tricolor—white, green, and red—we had a multitude of bicolors glistening in the sun—white and yellow. 

These "charms" decorated our train even when we stopped at stations in Bohemia and the people welcomed us with music, songs, bouquets, and welcoming speeches from mayors and other representatives. These yellow-and-white flags fluttered on the ropes even as our leader, Mr. Vasilaki, deafened the Czech listeners with his thunderous, sentimental speeches, and as Mr. Petko tickled the national pride of the brotherly Czech people at every station with his oratorical words, of which those standing further off could only clearly hear the words: "Brothers! Jan Hus... Oh! Jan Hus, brothers!", and when Bay Ganyo, indignant that the speeches made no mention of our own historical giants, poked a teacher in the ribs with the words: "Teacher, you say something too, man, let’s show them who we are, now’s the time, say something about either Philip Totyu or Krum the Terrible, or sing a song..." And the bicolor flags kept on fluttering!...

Our entire journey from the Czech border to Prague was one triumphal procession; whether past towns or villages, or through the fields—wherever our train passed, hats flew into the air and an endless “nazdar!” rent the air.

I noticed a woman working in the field who, seeing the men waving and throwing their hats, waved and waved her hands, then went and untied her headscarf, whirled it in the air, and shrieked: "Nazdar!" Another thing: we were passing by a town (I don't remember what it was called, and how could one remember, we were so dazed then), people in the streets, people at the windows, on the trees, on the fences, even on the eaves. So in this town, I remember, I noticed in one place a new house being built, almost finished, and the roof beams were laid out; at the peak of the roof, a long pole was stuck, adorned with greenery, and a flag at its tip (just like with us when houses are built): several workers up there, seeing that all along the street from every floor people were waving handkerchiefs and shouting "Nazdar!", ran along the beams toward the top of the roof, grabbed the pole with the flag, and tried to pull it out to salute us, but it seemed it was firmly fixed—they couldn't pull it out, but they shook it at its base enough so that it could sway with a small amplitude left and right. These two instances—with the worker in the field and the masons on the roof—moved me to the highest degree. It didn't resemble our usual: "The entire intelligentsia rent the air with frenetic cheers," "Today the whole nation rejoices..."

We arrived at the station in Prague. We did not notice many people on the platform; there were only official welcomers: the deputy mayor, if I am not mistaken, and the members of the exhibition committee. This reception seemed muted to me; we had grown accustomed to triumphs! But as it turned out, there was a reason for it; the people, being more organized, knew that when 160 people get off the train, if there is a crowd on the platform, they will get mixed up and confused: it would become a jumble of guests, hosts, and luggage, so they had left the platform empty and only a committee appeared to meet us. Greetings and speeches began again; on one side: "Brothers...! Bulgarians...! Great Slavic... Cyril and Methodius"; on another side: "Brothers, we have come to learn from the great Czech nation!"... on a third side: "Brothers! The great Jan Hus!... Yes, brothers, Jan Hus is great!" And Bay Ganyo, for his part, dissatisfied that they only mentioned Cyril and Methodius, nudged the teacher again: "You say something too, teacher! Don't we have plenty of our own? Tell them about Asparuh, or go on, blow the kaval—now's the time!..."

Here we were told that we would all go to the city club "Meshtanska Beseda," and from there we would be assigned to our lodgings. Arrangements were made for our luggage to be brought there. We set off. From the platform, we entered the station hall, and what a sight! People! Teeming with people! Literally, there wasn't a square inch of space. In the middle, there was a narrow lane, just wide enough for us to pass. On either side stood rows of ladies with bouquets, all dressed in their holiday best. Then a thunderous "Nazdar!" rang out, and they began handing us bouquets and showering us with flowers. When we stepped out onto the street and looked—good heavens!—as far as the eye could see, they had left only a narrow path for us, while everything else was jammed with people. And again, rows of ladies, and again "Nazdaaar! Nazdaaar! Hurrah!"—and again a hail of bouquets.

A royal welcome!... Amidst the shouts and the flowers, we climbed into carriages and set off. Now, as for how gracefully we seated ourselves and settled in with our families and nursing infants—I leave that to your imagination! We were absolutely thunderstruck by this unexpected, grand reception! We tipped our hats left and right; then we thought to take them off entirely (when it comes to being quick-witted, we were quite sharp, weren't we! We know how to handle these things, the etiquette!). A smile was frozen on my convulsively trembling lips, and I felt as though I wanted to laugh, to cry, and to sink into the ground all at once!

We arrived at the "Meshchanska Beseda" and took the tables in the garden. We were waiting for our luggage to arrive and to be assigned to our lodgings. Several carriage drivers waited, poor things, for a whole hour by the gates to be paid, but many of our tourists did not find it necessary to pay. "Big deal," Bay Ganyo was saying, "what does it cost them to pay for our carriages? After all—we are Slavs! This is where they should show their Slavic spirit, come on! Of course! Everything for free! With money, even a grandmother knows how! Just a bare—nazdar"…

The luggage arrived, and they began sending us off to our lodgings. People had taken the trouble to find us accommodations. I won't tell you about the quarrels with the coachmen, with the waiters at the club, with the organizers over delays or the accidental swapping of luggage, about the dissatisfaction with the lodgings, the haggling, and other such things. Let us transport ourselves for a moment into our room (do not be afraid, madam). The four of us settled into a large room. We had all the amenities. Our room looked out onto the courtyard... On the opposite side, an equal number of floors rose up. At one point, the maid who was attending to us, Anushka, as she was taking the flower pots off the windowsills so she could close them, suddenly turned to me and asked bashfully, gesturing with her eyes toward the windows opposite:

— Please, sir, is that gentleman also a Bulgarian? Do look at what he is doing! How dark he is! Hairy like some kind of savage! Ha-ha-ha-ha!

I look in the indicated direction, and what do I see? Bai Ganyo, with the windows wide open, without having drawn the curtains or the shutters, had stripped off his outer garments; and at the very moment I looked, he was leering at our maid and stroking his hairy chest, evidently intending to captivate her with this.

In the local newspapers that same day, greetings appeared for the dear (and they were right) guests — *bratri Bulhari*. The program according to which we were to visit the exhibition and the sights of the city of Prague was also printed. They published reports of our visits: where we had gone, how we had been received, how they had welcomed us, and what we had replied to them. The name of our leader, Mr. Vasilaki, was echoing everywhere; he earned this attention with his countless speeches. And to tell the truth, say what you will, but if it hadn't been for Mr. Vasilaki to gloss things over for them, we would have been a total failure.

At the entrance of the exhibition, we were met by members of the committee. And once again, speeches about *cesheho naroda*, about *bulharskeho naroda*. Here, you see, they didn't make the mistake of greeting us as Serbs—a blunder that, they say, occurred at the entrance of the Plovdiv Exhibition: the people of Sliven and Yambol were in constant antagonism—whether out of envy, rivalry, who knows what. The Sliven folk appeared at the entrance of the Plovdiv Exhibition, and a committee member delivered a speech to them, mistaking them for the Yambol folk, and how he praised them: "The brave people of Yambol, the glorious people of Yambol!" And the people of Sliven were sweating, coughing into their hands, blinking... Quite a sight!...

We entered the exposition. A member of the committee led us to take a quick general overview of the main departments. And who was he leading? Our tourists—veritable Englishmen!... Once those people of yours entered the botanical department, there was no getting them out!
— Ivancho, Ivancho, come, come here, look at this tulip, what a big one! Do you remember, your aunt has a tulip just like it! — one of them calls out from one side.
— Mariika, Mariika, come, come here, look, a mimosa, this is a mimosa, do you see? Do you remember in the little atlas I bought you for Easter? — another calls out from another side.
— Look at that, basil! Tsk... tsk... tsk... Even the Czechs have basil, bravo! — a third one chimes in, and they all rush over to look at the basil.
— Well, I don't see any geranium here — Bay Ganyo pipes up in a disgruntled voice, — a poor show, if they don't have any geranium! Ah, back home! In the Balkan mountains! Damn it all!
And the committee member meanwhile was on pins and needles! They were waiting for the dear guests to finish their talk!...

I could not restrain myself; I left the botanical department and went to gawk at the other pavilions. In my absence, the distinguished guests were photographed, and the next day the whole group appeared in an illustrated newspaper.

They took us to Hradčany, where the palaces of the Czech kings are. They showed us various historical nooks: the small room where the council met and the start of the Thirty Years' War was decided; the window through which the Czech patriots were thrown into the abyss. They took us to the Old Town Hall, to the old and the new museum. They staged an opera in our honor at the Národní divadlo and held a soiree at the "Měšťanská beseda." We visited Pan Náprstek, a highly respected citizen who was once compromised in the eyes of the Austrian government, fled to America, made a fortune there, returned to Prague, and now, surrounded by honors and respect, occupies himself with philanthropy. He has his own museum and library. Our host welcomed us with all the cordiality and hospitality of a Slav. Here, the most heartfelt speeches were made. In one of the rooms, there was a thick book in which visitors signed their names. At one point, when many people had crowded around the book and everyone was rushing to grab the pen and immortalize their name, Bay Ganyo pulled me by the sleeve and asked impatiently:

— Hey, what are they signing up for there?

Knowing beforehand that no pretext for signing would satisfy Bai Ganyo unless there was something in it for his belly, I told him jokingly: whoever does not wish to tour the antiquities of Prague any further may sign this book and have lunch at Mr. Naprstek’s.

— Is that so? — cried Bay Ganyo. — To the devil with their antiquities, give me the pen! Give it here, man, give me the pen quickly! Can't I use a pencil? Give it, give it, I'm in a hurry! — and he began to elbow his way toward the table on which the large book lay. They stepped on each other's toes, he jostled with someone, they began to snatch the pen from one another, they splattered the book with ink, and at last the trembling, hairy, and sweaty hand of Bay Ganyo adorned one of the pages with two resonant words: Ganyo Balkanski.
Tsvyatko told us that he did not wish to continue his story.
— Tell us something about the party. Didn't you say they gave a party in honor of the Bulgarians? — one of the group spoke up.

— I didn’t go to that soiree. Bay Ganyo did. A propos, that day I went with Bay Ganyo to a barbershop. He intended to captivate the Czech ladies that evening and was taking all sorts of preliminary measures to appear in all his glory: he bought a tie, cleaned his medal (for what did you expect of your Bay Ganyo!) and we went to the barbershop, because his hair and beard were quite overgrown. He sat in the chair. The barber carefully wrapped him up and began his work. We were delayed there for nearly a whole hour. It wasn't so easy to please Bay Ganyo.

— Here, here; tell him right here — and Bay Ganyo points to his neck — to smooth it out here, to scrape a bit with the razor. And tell him to keep his eyes peeled, not to nick any pimple, or there’ll be hell to pay.
The barber sees the angry expression on Bay Ganyo's sweaty face in the mirror and looks at me in bewilderment.

— Co pan mluvi? — he asks me humbly, thinking he has committed some blunder against Bay Ganyo’s taste.

— You there, tell him to put the talk aside for now — Bay Ganyo turns to me, in a tone as if he had hired me as his interpreter. — Tell him to leave me a goatee and have him make it a bit pointier, like Napoleon’s, you understand? And as for the mustache, let him comb it so it puffs up like — heh-heh! — the Italian king’s, hee-hee-hee! Have you seen him in portraits? That’s how he should make them! Tell him, come on!

I did not have the courage to translate Bay Ganyo’s modest wish literally; it would have put the barber in a great predicament: was it an easy task, with the help of a razor and a comb, to make someone resemble both Napoleon III and Humbert! And whom, of all people!

The grooming was finished. Bay Ganyo pulled out his purse, unwound the string, opened it, reached to the bottom, scooped up a handful of coins, turned his back to us, rummaged and rummaged through the coins, chose one and handed it to the barber, but he handed it in such a way as if to say: “Here, take it, never mind, let it be on me.” The coin was twenty kreuzers. But realizing he might have made a mistake, and so they wouldn't think him a fool, he gestured with his fingers toward the barber, as if to say “give me change.” In an instant, the barber opened the drawer, threw the coin in, picked out two ten-kreuzer coins, slammed them angrily onto the marble table, and disappeared through an inner door. The coins rolled onto the floor. At first, Bay Ganyo seemed a bit startled, a bit puzzled, but I couldn't quite catch that impression before he bent down, picked up the money, and said:

— Angry Petko—his bag is empty! Come on, forget them! All they know is how to fleece you! Don't I know them! Slavs!... Nonsense!...
